title: Fill to the line, biggest jugs first
allegory: Top-p is like pouring jugs of water into a bucket, biggest first, until the water reaches a line, then holding a raffle among only the jugs you poured, weighted by their water.
map: pouring until the water reaches the line
adding probabilities until the running total reaches p
the jug that crosses the line still counts
inclusive cutoff: keep the token where the total first reaches p
a raffle among the poured jugs, weighted by water
renormalise the kept probabilities and sample
one huge jug fills it fast; tiny jugs take many pours
the nucleus shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is unsure

props.label: always the likeliest: 'I don't know. I don't know.'
anything goes: 'the cat sat on the quantum'

cap.1: Always pick the likeliest next word and text turns bland and loops. Pick from everything and weird rare words sneak in. You want the sensible middle.
cap.2: Holtzman et al. (ICLR 2020): likelihood is a great training objective and a poor decoding one. Maximising it gives bland, repetitive text; the unreliable tail gives nonsense. Trim, then sample.
cap.3: Degeneration: maximisation-style decoding from an excellent model yields repetitive text, and human text doesn't look like high-likelihood text. Truncating the tail keeps diversity without the junk.

cap.1: Line up jugs of water, biggest first. Pour them into a bucket until the water reaches the line. Then hold a raffle among the jugs you poured.
cap.2: Sort tokens by probability, add them up until the running total reaches p, keep those, renormalise and sample. The line is p; the poured jugs are the nucleus.
cap.3: Nucleus = the smallest top-ranked set with cumulative mass ≥ p; sample from it renormalised. Its size is decided afresh each step by the shape of the distribution.

cap.1: Jugs of 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, line at 0.8. Two jugs reach only 0.7, so the third is poured too. The last jug sits out; the raffle is among three.
cap.2: ARENA's example: (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) with p = 0.8 keeps three tokens, because two only reach 0.7. You then sample from (0.4, 0.3, 0.2) / 0.9.
cap.3: Kept mass 0.9 ≥ 0.8. Renormalised: 0.444, 0.333, 0.222. The fourth token's mass is dropped and the survivors scale up by 1/0.9.

chapters.name: Confident or unsure

left.title: confident step
lines: one jug holds most of the water

chapters.verdict: Top-k keeps a fixed count; top-p keeps a fixed mass, so its cutoff moves with confidence.

cap.1: When one jug is huge, a couple of pours fill the bucket. When every jug is small, you need many. The raffle sizes itself to how sure the model is.
cap.2: Top-k keeps a fixed count; top-p keeps a fixed mass, so its cutoff moves with the model's confidence. On a flat distribution a fixed k cuts far too much.
cap.3: Nucleus size tracks the distribution's spread: peaked steps keep a handful, flat steps can keep hundreds. Lower temperature sharpens probabilities before the cumsum, so it shrinks the nucleus too.

cap.1: The jug that crosses the line still counts. Check the water already in before each pour, and the first jug always gets poured: never an empty raffle.
cap.2: Keep token i if the total before it is below p. The first token always qualifies, so the set is never empty. Test: GPT-2 on 'John and Mary went to the' at p = 0.1 keeps ' church' and ' house'.
cap.3: Inclusive: keep up to the first index where cumsum ≥ p. The exclusive version is empty whenever p_max > p (any p below 0.0648 on that prompt) and crashes Categorical. Add min_tokens_to_keep as a floor.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: top_p is a slider in every generation API
Same model, new decoder, different text
Record sampling settings with every result

cap.1: You'll meet top_p as a slider in almost every AI tool. Now you know what it does: it trims the unlikely tail, by mass, afresh at every word.
cap.2: Decoding alone changes output quality from the same model, so many 'bad model' complaints are really 'bad decoder' ones. Top-p is a library knob: know what it does, set it, move on.
cap.3: When you evaluate or steer behaviour, sampling settings are part of the measurement: the same weights under different decoders give different behaviour. Log them with every result.

coda.title: The cat sat on the ___: drag p and the temperature
coda.f: (() => { const q = softmax([3, 2.2, 1.6, 1.1, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1, -0.2].map(v => v/T)); let before = 0; const keep = q.map(v => { const k = before < p; before += v; return k; }); const Z = sum(q.filter((v, i) => keep[i])); return q.map((v, i) => keep[i] ? v/Z : 0); })()

readouts.label: words in the raffle (the nucleus)
readouts.f: (() => { const q = softmax([3, 2.2, 1.6, 1.1, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1, -0.2].map(v => v/T)); let before = 0, n = 0; q.forEach(v => { if (before < p) n++; before += v; }); return n; })()

readouts.label: water poured before renormalising
readouts.f: (() => { const q = softmax([3, 2.2, 1.6, 1.1, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1, -0.2].map(v => v/T)); let before = 0, m = 0; q.forEach(v => { if (before < p) m += v; before += v; }); return m.toFixed(3); })()

caption.1: Drag p and watch words join or leave the raffle. Then drag the temperature: a confident model needs fewer words to reach the same line.
caption.2: Bars show the renormalised nucleus. Low p or low temperature keeps few words; high p or high temperature keeps many. 'mat' is always in: the cutoff is inclusive.
caption.3: Nucleus size depends on both p and T: lowering T sharpens the softmax before the cumsum and shrinks the support. The inclusive cut guarantees at least one token for any p > 0.

hamming.what: A sampling rule that keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities reach p, renormalises them, and samples.
hamming.when: Whenever you generate text and want variety without the unreliable tail, usually as a top_p setting.
hamming.why: Likelihood is a poor decoding objective, and cutting by mass adapts to the model's confidence where a fixed count cannot.

object.title: The nucleus terrace
object.subtitle: Six moments in a sentence, each a row of next-word chances; words outside the nucleus sink to stubs.
object.f: (() => { const q = softmax(range(cols).map(k => -k*[1.6, 1.0, 0.6, 0.35, 0.18, 0.06][r]/T)); let before = 0; for (let i = 0; i < c; i++) before += q[i]; return before < p ? 0.08 + 2.2*q[c] : 0.02; })()

cap.1: Six moments in a sentence, one per row, from sure to clueless. Each row's bars are the next-word chances, biggest first. Stubs are words cut from the raffle.
cap.2: Each row is one step's sorted distribution; stubs are tokens outside the nucleus.
cap.3: Rows vary in entropy; the nucleus at p = 0.9 is the tall prefix of each row.

cap.1: Same p for every row, yet the sure row keeps 2 words and the clueless row keeps 9.
cap.2: At p = 0.9 the nucleus sizes run 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 from the most to the least confident row.
cap.3: Fixed mass, variable count: |nucleus| rises monotonically with the row's entropy.

cap.1: Lower the line to 0.5: every row keeps fewer words, and the two surest rows keep just one.
cap.3: Small p approaches greedy decoding on peaked rows while leaving flat rows some diversity.

cap.1: Back to 0.9, but cool the temperature: the chances sharpen and most rows need fewer words to reach the same line.
cap.2: T = 0.5 at p = 0.9 shrinks sizes to 1, 2, 2, 4, 6, 9.
cap.3: Temperature rescales logits before the cumsum, so T and p jointly set the effective support.

cap.1: Push the line to 0.99 and nearly everything is back in, junk tail included.
cap.2: p near 1 approaches plain sampling: sizes 3, 5, 8, 10, 10, 10.
cap.3: As p → 1 the truncation vanishes and the unreliable tail returns.

predict.q: Probabilities (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) and p = 0.8. How many tokens are kept?
predict.why: Two only reach 0.7, below 0.8, so the third is kept too: the crossing token counts.

predict.q: Your sample_top_p crashes, but only for tiny p. Most likely bug?

options.t: The cutoff is exclusive, so the kept set can be empty

predict.why: If the top token alone exceeds p, an exclusive cut keeps nothing. Keep up to and including the token where the total first reaches p.

predict.q: Same p, but the model is very unsure. What happens to the nucleus?

options.t: It grows: many small chances are needed to reach p

predict.why: Top-p fixes the mass, not the count, so a flat distribution needs more tokens.

object.where: Any 'fewest items covering p of the total' rule, such as picking how many PCA components to keep.
